desc:
The array nums is sorted in non-decreasing order and may contain repeated values. Count the distinct pairs of values (x, y) with y - x = k such that x and y can be taken from two different positions of the array.

Two pairs are the same when they have the same (x, y), however many times those values occur. For k = 0 a value counts only when it occurs at least twice.

nums = [1, 1, 3, 3, 5, 5, 5, 7], k = 2
distinct value pairs: (1,3) (3,5) (5,7)
result = 3
hints: A set of seen values answers the question for k > 0, but there is a sorted array to exploit and k = 0 needs extra care. Think about two pointers that both move forward.
Let i point at a value x and j at the first element after i with a[j] - a[i] ≥ k. When i advances, can j ever need to move backwards?
No: both pointers only move right. Skip an i whose value equals the previous one, force j > i, and count when a[j] - a[i] == k.
editorial: Walk i over the array but process each distinct value only once (skip i when a[i] == a[i-1]). Keep j as the first index after i with a[j] - a[i] ≥ k. If that difference equals k exactly, the value pair (a[i], a[i]+k) exists: count it.

Because the array is sorted, a larger i never needs an earlier j, so j never moves back and both pointers travel at most n steps: O(n) time, O(1) space. Forcing j ≥ i + 1 makes the case k = 0 work by itself: it only counts when another element equal to a[i] follows it.
A hash set also works in O(n) but needs O(n) memory and a separate branch for k = 0.
